original_question: Suppose the natural numbers are finitely coloured. Determine whether there must exist two infinite sets A and B of natural numbers such that every product ab and every sum a+b with a in A and b in B has the same colour.
target_in_paper: Section 7 (Ramsey Theory), Question 7.2 (F. Richter, Ultramath 2022, Pisa.): given any finite colouring of the natural numbers, do there exist infinite sets A and B of natural numbers such that {ab : a ∈ A, b ∈ B} ∪ {a + b : a ∈ A, b ∈ B} is monochromatic?
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the right target almost exactly: it uses a finite colouring of the natural numbers, asks for two infinite sets A and B, and requires one common colour for all cross-products ab and all cross-sums a+b. That is the substance of Question 7.2.
missing_details: The paper phrases the condition as the single set {ab : a ∈ A, b ∈ B} ∪ {a + b : a ∈ A, b ∈ B} being monochromatic; this makes explicit that the same colour must work simultaneously for both the product-part and the sum-part.
To make the problem fully stand-alone, the finite colouring can be written explicitly as a map c: N -> {1,...,r} for some r ≥ 1, or equivalently as an arbitrary finite colouring of N.
It should be stated explicitly that A and B are subsets of the natural numbers and that both are infinite.
No extra hypotheses appear in the paper: A and B are not required to be disjoint, ordered, or distinct from one another, and there is no distinctness condition on the values a+b or ab.
refined_question: Let c: N -> {1,...,r} be a finite colouring of the natural numbers, for some integer r ≥ 1. Must there exist infinite sets A,B ⊆ N such that the set {ab : a ∈ A, b ∈ B} ∪ {a + b : a ∈ A, b ∈ B} is monochromatic under c?
justification: The draft is aiming at Section 7, Ramsey Theory, Question 7.2, not Question 7.1: the official problem is exactly about finding two infinite sets A and B whose cross-products and cross-sums all lie in a single colour class. The sentence immediately after Question 7.2 explains the intended scope, presenting it as an infinitary question motivated by known partition-regularity results for sums-and-products configurations over the natural numbers and the rationals. I therefore kept the reformulation narrow and faithful to that exact question.
